title: Khanmigo Doesn't Love Kids
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer builds a pointed critique of Khan Academy's Khanmigo AI tutor around a simple, repeatable experiment: he types a mathematically substantive but partially incorrect answer to a find-the-equation-of-a-line problem, then asks Khanmigo for help, doing this a dozen times over. In every case, Khanmigo responds as though the student had contributed nothing - restarting from the very beginning of the procedure and never acknowledging the parts of the answer that were correct, which Meyer finds more galling than an outright wrong response would be. He frames this using the software-design concept of hostile user design, arguing the failure isn't incidental but structural: Khanmigo's underlying prompt evidently never injects the student's actual answer into the model's context, so the AI has no way to recognize or build on what the student already understood. To sharpen the contrast, Meyer crowdsources the same scenario to real teachers on Twitter and finds every single response starts by naming what the student got right before addressing the error - a basic move Khanmigo never manages across a dozen tries. He then demonstrates the fix is straightforward from an engineering standpoint, rewriting a ChatGPT prompt that explicitly includes the student's answer alongside the correct one, which immediately produces responses that acknowledge partial correctness - underscoring his argument that Khanmigo's failure to serve students is a deliberate or careless design choice, not a technical ceiling.
points: Meyer's diagnostic method is deliberately simple and reproducible: type a wrong-but-substantive answer into Khanmigo a dozen times and observe it repeatedly ignore the content of the student's actual attempt.
He borrows the software-design concept of "hostile user design" to argue Khanmigo's failure isn't a bug but a structural choice - the tool doesn't extract or value the student's own input at all.

His crowdsourced comparison (real teachers on Twitter responding to the identical wrong answer) shows every human response starting by naming what the student got right, a baseline Khanmigo never met across a dozen attempts.

Meyer demonstrates the fix is trivial from an engineering standpoint - a rewritten prompt that explicitly injects the student's answer alongside the correct one produces responses that acknowledge partial correctness.
quotes: In software, the concept of “hostile user design” is well understood. Software that doesn’t understand or value its users.
I would not presume to know what lives in the heart of Sal Khan or anyone else working at Khan Academy, but I know that Khanmigo does not love students. This is easy to illustrate.
Every time, Khanmigo treated me as though I knew absolutely nothing of value about the equation of a line.
That last one hurt especially. 'Can you tell me the y-intercept from the graph?' Yes! I told it to you already. It's the one part of my answer that's fully correct!

I went on Twitter and asked teachers there what feedback they’d give that same student. Every one of dozens of responses started with what the kid knew. They started with a recognition of the kid’s value.
It’s clear that however Khan Academy is prompting ChatGPT, they are not injecting the student’s answer into the prompt. The model has no appreciation or even awareness of the student’s thinking here.
